factSheet.title: Nigeria's National AI Strategy: five pillars, a 70% skills target and an execution gap

claims.text: Nigeria launched its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in Lagos in April 2025, according to Nairametrics.

The strategy is built on five pillars: building AI infrastructure, fostering an innovation ecosystem, driving AI adoption across sectors, ensuring responsible AI development, and establishing robust governance.
A four-day workshop in Abuja brought together over 120 AI researchers and practitioners to draft the strategy, according to the Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy.
A draft of the strategy was published in August 2024.
The strategy cites a target to equip 70% of youth with AI-related skills.
claims.label: Youth AI-skills target

claims.text: Short-term items include setting up governance bodies, seeding demonstration projects, a national AI skills drive and pilot high-performance computing infrastructure.
A policy brief by Tunani finds the strategy has few binding commitments, measurable targets or dedicated budget lines.
The brief says Nigeria spends 0.2% of GDP on research and development.
claims.label: Nigeria

claims.text: It puts the global average at 2.2% of GDP.
claims.label: Global average

claims.text: The brief says Nigeria has advanced on talent, through the 3MTT programme and the N-ATLAS language model, but lags peers on infrastructure, governance and R&D spending.
Minister Bosun Tijani has presented a vision for a National AI Trust at a convening hosted by Warwick Business School in London, describing it as the first institution of its kind in the world.
He is also raising $2 billion for Project BRIDGE, an initiative to lay 90,000 kilometres of fibre-optic cable across Nigeria.

In 2024 the ministry said Galaxy Backbone would partner with 21st Century Technologies on a national compute project open to local researchers, startups and government entities working on AI projects of national interest.

article:
> **Key takeaways**
>
> - Nigeria launched its National AI Strategy in Lagos in April 2025, after a draft was published in August 2024. [c1][c4]
> - The strategy has five pillars, from infrastructure and ecosystem to adoption, responsible AI and governance. [c2]
> - It cites a target to equip 70% of youth with AI-related skills. [c5]
> - A Tunani policy brief finds few binding commitments, measurable targets or dedicated budget lines. [c7]

## The landscape shift

Nigeria drafted the strategy with its AI community. A four-day workshop in Abuja brought together over 120 AI researchers and practitioners, according to the ministry. [c3] A draft was published in August 2024, [c4] and the strategy was launched in Lagos in April 2025. [c1]

## What the strategy sets out

### The five pillars

The strategy is built on five pillars: building AI infrastructure, fostering an innovation ecosystem, driving AI adoption across sectors, ensuring responsible AI development, and establishing robust governance. [c2]

### Early steps

- Short-term items include setting up governance bodies, seeding demonstration projects, a national AI skills drive and pilot high-performance computing infrastructure. [c6]
- It cites a target to equip 70% of youth with AI-related skills. [c5]
- In 2024 the ministry said Galaxy Backbone would partner with 21st Century Technologies on a national compute project open to local researchers, startups and government entities working on AI projects of national interest. [c13]

## Where Nigeria stands

| Measure | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Nigeria's R&D spending | 0.2% of GDP | [c8] |
| Global average | 2.2% of GDP | [c9] |

## Limits of the evidence

The Tunani policy brief finds the strategy has few binding commitments, measurable targets or dedicated budget lines. [c7] It says Nigeria has advanced on talent, through the 3MTT programme and the N-ATLAS language model, but lags peers on infrastructure, governance and R&D spending. [c10]

## What comes next

- Minister Bosun Tijani has presented a vision for a National AI Trust at a convening hosted by Warwick Business School in London, describing it as the first institution of its kind in the world. [c11]
- He is also raising $2 billion for Project BRIDGE, an initiative to lay 90,000 kilometres of fibre-optic cable across Nigeria. [c12]
